title: How to Learn Responsibly About Palestine
subtitle: A practical method for checking reports, images, dates, and claims
summary: Reports about Palestine move quickly and often carry strong emotion. A responsible reader pauses, finds the original source, checks the date and place, looks for independent confirmation, and labels uncertainty honestly before sharing. Quran 49:6 makes verification part of preventing harm.

sections.title: Check Before You Share
sections.body: Care for Palestinians should deepen a commitment to truth, not weaken it. Quran 49:6 tells believers to investigate reports so that people are not harmed through ignorance. A false caption, invented quotation, or outdated number can harm innocent people and discredit a just concern.

sections.title: Six Checks Before You Share
sections.body:
- Find the original: who first published the words, image, video, or number?
- Check the date: is old material being presented as new?
- Check the place: do landmarks, weather, language, and reliable geolocation support the caption?
- Inspect the evidence: is the full document or unedited footage available?
- Seek independent confirmation: does another credible source with its own evidence support the central claim?
- State the confidence level: confirmed, alleged, disputed, corrected, or still unverified.

The [Verification Handbook](https://verificationhandbook.com/) gives step-by-step methods for digital material. Verification does not require ignoring suffering. It helps prevent a true cause from being defended with a false claim.

sections.title: Images, Numbers, and Quotations Need Different Checks
sections.body:
For an image, search for earlier copies, compare landmarks, and look for the original uploader. For video, examine key frames and listen for language or sounds that may locate it. Cropping and missing context can mislead even when the image itself is real.

For casualty or aid figures, identify the organization, date, method, population counted, and later revisions. For quotations, open the full speech or document and read the sentences around the excerpt. A screenshot of text is not a source. UNESCO's [handbook on journalism and disinformation](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/journalism-fake-news-disinformation) explains practical fact-checking and social-media verification.

sections.title: Use the Right Source for the Question
sections.body:
Primary documents establish what an institution officially said; they do not automatically prove that every statement in the document is true. Historians reconstruct events from many records. Human-rights investigators assess evidence under stated methods. News reports document events while information is still developing. Religious texts explain belief and moral duty. Courts interpret law in particular proceedings. No single source type answers every question.

Apply the same standard to claims that support your position and claims that challenge it. Responsible learning is not false neutrality. It is disciplined truthfulness for the sake of justice.

sections.title: Truthful Advocacy Is Stronger Advocacy
sections.body: A helpful advocate is careful with evidence, transparent about uncertainty, and unwilling to use another person's suffering as a slogan. Verify first, speak precisely, correct mistakes openly, and keep human dignity at the center. This is stronger advocacy and better Islamic character.

quranVerses.arabic: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ إِن جَآءَكُمْ فَاسِقٌۢ بِنَبَإٍۢ فَتَبَيَّنُوٓا۟ أَن تُصِيبُوا۟ قَوْمًۢا بِجَهَٰلَةٍۢ فَتُصْبِحُوا۟ عَلَىٰ مَا فَعَلْتُمْ نَٰدِمِينَ
quranVerses.translation: O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.
